newsitem.title: UK: Amended UK inflation target no cause for concern.
newsitem.headline: Amended UK inflation target no cause for concern.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's amendments to the inflation target represent a slight loosening of the monetary stance, but they are unlikely to have any adverse practical consequences, economists said.

Brown said the target for underlying inflation would remain unchanged at 2.5 percent but deviations of more than one percentage point on either side would require an explanatory letter from the Bank of England.
"It is quite clearly a loosening of the monetary stance when compared with a 2.5 percent ceiling," said Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse.
"The question is, is it an unwarranted loosening of policy? I would say no. I think it is consistent with what most pragmatic economists would like to see."
Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc, said that in practice the one percent band was unlikely to make any difference.
"The band should be wide enough for the Bank to consistently remain within it but for the time being, the reality is the authorities have struggled to meet the target exactly," he said.
Brown told parliament he had tightened the monetary framework and made it more rigorous.
Simon Briscoe of Nikko Europe Plc was unconvinced.
"The apparently strict monetary policy regime that was unveiled a month ago is now being diluted," he said.
"It unambiguously implies less strong monetary policy than the market had priced in when the first stab at the new regime was announced a month ago."
Briscoe believes the reforms could lead to more frequent changes in interest rates and less long-term stability in both interest and exchange rates.

Jonathan Loynes of HSBC Markets said the changes did amount to a slight softening in the inflation target but he did not believe they would result in significantly higher inflation than would otherwise have been the case.
"I think there was a need for some lower limit to prevent the Bank of England from going into overkill on interest rates."
A Treasury source told Reuters the government aimed to avoid a deflationary bias to monetary policy.
Ciaran Barr of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said the likelihood of inflation dipping as low as 1.5 percent in the next few years was slim.
"It is very difficult in Britain to get inflation as low as that," he said.

Barr also believes the Bank's quarterly Inflation Reports show it is not blindly committed to fighting inflation at any cost. "I think the Bank is pragmatic and never really came across as trying to get rid of inflation altogether."
Jeffrey of Charterhouse said the changes went some way towards alleviating his worries about the Bank of England's control of interest rates.
"If you have a ceiling as a target you are bound to shoot low," he said.
As for the new implied inflation target range of 1.5 percent to 3.5 percent, this did not appear unacceptable.

Jeffrey's concern is the potential inflationary impact of around 30 billion stg of "windfalls" which millions of Britons will receive this year as mutually owned building societies and insurance companies float on the stock exchange.
"The real danger is that the windfalls prove incredibly potent and that inflation has a little bit of a kick to it later this year," he said.

"My concern is that the Governor is going to be writing a letter explaining why inflation is higher than one percent above the band within a relatively short period of time. It wouldn't surprise me if he was writing that letter before the end of the year."
